text.p: Base metals prices largely trended higher during Thursday LME trading, although the pace of business was mostly routine with prices generally rangebound.
Gold closed easier, grains were generally higher and oil was firm. The CRB index was up 1.68 points higher at 246.43.

Copper, which was successfully supported at $2,300 on Wednesday, consistently pushed higher but stalled at intermediate resistance around $2,350. News that unions at Poland's KGHM were on strike alert was supportive, but did not over-exite the market which is still ranging between $2,320/30 and $2,380 on the upside. At the end of the kerb three months prices were at $2,351.50, up $26.50 a tonne from Wednesday. The cash/threes backwardation widened to around $39/44, against $36.

Aluminium prices were firmer, partly helped by copper, but also bouyed by short-covering after Wednesday's support at $1,650. The market was also helped by a headline drop in February IPAI daily production, although some analysts doubted the veracity of recent data which now includes Chinese figures.
Angus MacMillan of LME trader Billiton Metals Ltd noted that the IPAI data suggested that overall Asian production had fallen.
However, China's State Statistical Bureau said today that China production in Jan/Feb rose 23.5 percent.

"The implication is that IPAI production fell elsewhere in Asia," he said. But output elsewhere in the region is being maintained, so the data that has been added this year to the IPAI is increasingly suspect.
By the close of the kerb prices were $16 steadier at $1,669 - well above the early low of $1,650.
Nickel prices perked up during the session, also helped by trends in copper, with the market edging back above $8,000. Last trade was at $8,040, up $55 from the previous kerb.
Lead and zinc were both steadier throughout the session although the former metal drifted back towards the lower end of the day's range on the kerb to close at $694, up just $3.
However, zinc remained reasonably well supported above $1,300 and poised to test recent 4-1/2 year highs. The market closed at $1,305, up $9.

COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended mixed Thursday, with gold and silver closing lower, but platinum group metals edging higher. "Investors continue to be bargain hunters at prices below $350 an ounce (in gold)," said Ted Kempf, analyst with New York based CPM Group. "Still this is a highly technical market and the shorts seem intent of forcing prices below $350 target, with $340 as the key technical objective on the downside," he said. "Any sell off is expected to be brief, considering the level of small bar demand at these levels."
COMEX April gold ended down 70 cents at $352.30 an ounce, after seeing a $351.20-354.40 range.
In the bullion market spot gold ended quoted $351.30/80, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $352.00 and the New York close Wednesday around $351.80/20.
Earlier this week gold prices slipped back below $350 an ounce, after recovering to around $365 in the past month from a three year low at $336.
But good underlying physical demand, signs of a topping out in the US dollar, and weakness in US stocks and bonds this week, are all providing some support for precious metals, traders said.
CBOT wheat futures closed higher on fund buying and a potential for flooding this spring in the U.S. Midwest, traders said. The fund buying was estimated at 15.0 million bushels.
Spring flooding in the U.S. Midwest could damage some of the U.S. winter wheat crop and delay seeding of the spring wheat crop, traders said.

Some traders said the surge in the soybean complex was central to the gains in wheat futures with the soy complex pits boosted by fund buying, CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed two to 12 cents per bushel higher, with May up 6-1/2 at $3.97-1/2.
NYMEX crude was firm on Thursday afternoon on buying in the nearby calendar spread ahead of April crude's expiry at session's end. April crude settled up 28 cents at $22.

CSCE world sugar futures settled firmer but well off the highs amid brisk activity. Dealers attributed gains to technically-driven local and fund short-covering coupled with a lack of selling, in early activity. The spot month May closed up 0.15 cent at 10.90 cents per lb. 32 a barrel.
